children.text: This is an artifact of doing as the platform is documented to work. You can do what the man page says, or you can do the opposite. The whole article is about how forking on macOS is troublesome.
This doesn't allow reusing initialization work via CoW mappings (like GP was asking about).
The manpage suggests if you need the child to be the same as the parent to exec a copy of the parent in the child right after forking.

children.author: zbentley
children.text: It looks like threads and a copy-on-write data structure or memory mapping.
But what would the equivalent "do the expensive preparation 1 time, then re-use copy-on-write memory N times" pattern look like, after reconsidering my life?

fork() was always very restricted in when it could be used and really dangerous even then. It was made for a world where process == thread, and since that ceased to be true it's been a large footgun. Use spawn if you need to launch a process, reconsider your life if your immediate post-fork() syscall is not exec()

children.text: I believe what's being described in the article is the same reason why some shells like fish also use posix_spawn() on macOS instead of fork/exec. Not only is it much faster, but it's also effectively problem-free for multi-threaded applications

children.author: cestith
children.text:
The man page on macOS suggests that if you need the child to be a copy of the parent like you’d get after fork(), that you can fork() then exec() the same program in the child. That gives it enough independence to be safe.

Using fork() without exec() was once a tried and true way to have a parent manage one or more children that just run a different branch of the code after the fork. It doesn’t work as well when you have a lot of async and a lot of fired signals right after forking, though. It gets worse if your signal handlers do more than, for example, assigning a value to a scalar variable and that’s honestly partially true of signal handlers no matter whether you’ve forked or not. That’s probably why Go blocks signals during that time after a fork(), for better or worse. So, TL;DR, if you need to run a child with the same code as the parent, exec() a copy like the manpage suggests especially on macOS.

It’s a shame old Unix code that used this model won’t work as well as they used to across different Unix flavors. At least it's not much hassle to fix.
